# Finding $\lim_{t\to\infty} e^{At}$ for a General Square Matrix $A$

## Step 1: Diagonalize (or Jordan-decompose) $A$

Assume $A \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$. By the Jordan theorem, $A = PJP^{-1}$ where $J$ is the Jordan canonical form. Then:

$$e^{At} = P\,e^{Jt}\,P^{-1}$$

## Step 2: Analyze a single Jordan block

For a Jordan block $J_k(\lambda) = \lambda I_k + N$ (where $N$ is nilpotent of index $\le k$):

$$e^{J_k(\lambda)\,t} = e^{\lambda t}\,e^{Nt} = e^{\lambda t}\!\left(I + Nt + \frac{(Nt)^2}{2!} + \cdots\right)$$

Each entry is of the form $p(t)\,e^{\lambda t}$ where $p(t)$ is a polynomial in $t$.

## Step 3: Determine the limit of $p(t)\,e^{\lambda t}$ as $t\to\infty$

| Condition on $\lambda$ | Behaviour of $e^{\lambda t}$ | Limit of $p(t)e^{\lambda t}$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda) < 0$ | decays to $0$ exponentially | $0$ (exponential dominates any polynomial) |
| $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda) = 0$ | oscillates / constant | does **not** converge (unless $\lambda=0$ and block is $1\times1$) |
| $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda) > 0$ | grows exponentially | diverges to $\infty$ |

## Step 4: Combine all blocks

Since $P$ and $P^{-1}$ are fixed, the limit $\lim_{t\to\infty}e^{At}$ **exists** if and only if **every** eigenvalue of $A$ has strictly negative real part:

$$\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_i) < 0 \quad \text{for all } i=1,\dots,n.$$

In that case every entry of $e^{At}$ tends to $0$, so:

$$\lim_{t\to\infty} e^{At} = P\,\mathbf{0}\,P^{-1} = \mathbf{0}.$$

If any $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_i)\ge 0$, the limit does not exist (or diverges).

## Final Result

$$\boxed{\lim_{t \to \infty} \mathrm{e}^{At} = \mathbf{0} \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \operatorname{Re}(\lambda_i) < 0 \;\;\forall\, i,}$$

i.e., the limit is the **zero matrix** precisely when $A$ is a **Hurwitz (stable) matrix**.
